bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body: Supply chain disruptions (shipping congestion/costs to KSA); Execution delays in EPC due to POCM timing; Geopolitical tension in West Asia; Diesel price volatility; Margin dilution from EPC mix.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident and aggressive on expansion (doubling down on KSA despite geopolitics); Transparent on margin mix shifts; Disciplined on EPC contract selection to protect ROCE.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: The 'margin decline' is a mathematical artifact of adding a high-ROCE, low-margin EPC business to a high-margin rental book, not a deterioration in core operating efficiency. KSA business is already monthly EBITDA positive, faster than expected.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- The Elevate 2030 capital model shifts "Asset-heavy -> Hybrid Model": FY26 achievement is "SFRPL - High ROCE asset light business complements SML asset heavy business" and the FY27 target is an explicit "Pivot to capital allocator", with strategy "Reshaping ELEVATE 2030 to focus on the capital pivot model".
- Leverage discipline: net debt to equity of 0.23, 0.19, 0.28, 0.33 and 0.47 over FY22-FY26, described as "Net Debt to Equity maintained below 0.5x"; guidance raises the "D/E Ceiling (x)" to 0.72 for FY27 and 0.76-0.80 for FY28 (Q1 FY26 0.40, Q1 FY27 0.54).
- Returns: ROCE of 6%, 16%, 21%, 17%, 15% over FY22-FY26 ("Double digit ROCE"); Q1 FY27 group ROCE 16% and ROE 15% (both marked "*ROCE & ROE as on 31-Mar-26"), with segment ROCE of 15% (Crane Rental), -6% (GCC Crane Rental) and 77% (Renewables E&C).
- Cash generation: cash profit of Rs 148 / 233 / 320 / 285 / 324 Cr over FY22-FY26, captioned "Average Rs 250 Cr+ Cash Profit in last 5 years"; Q1 FY27 group cash profit Rs 104 Cr.
- Guidance (consolidated) sets FY27 total income at Rs 1,400-1,500 Cr and FY28 at Rs 1,800-1,900 Cr, EBITDA of Rs 525-575 Cr (FY27) and Rs 650-700 Cr (FY28), against FY26 actuals of Rs 1,100 Cr income and Rs 429 Cr EBITDA; blended ROCE guided to 16.25-16.5% (FY27) and 16.5-17.0% (FY28) versus 16% in FY26.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Disciplined balance sheet as a strategic advantage - consistently low leverage and return-led capital allocation stated to enable growth without compromising balance sheet strength, resilience in downcycles and flexibility to invest ahead of demand
- Demand-backed expansion with superior asset productivity - fleet expansion aligned with visible demand, supported by a stated order book and inquiry pipeline, with a focus on yield and asset productivity
- High revenue visibility - a structurally high proportion of revenues secured at the start of the year, stated ~50% historical visibility trend and 40-45% repeat business share
- Execution-led customer relationships driving repeat business - stated ability to execute complex, large-scale projects has produced long-standing relationships described as a competitive moat
- Asset-light renewables platform - execution-led, capital-efficient participation in renewables stated to diversify earnings without incremental asset intensity
- Scale of fleet and engineering depth - 550+ cranes in fleet, 200+ specialised transport equipment, in-house engineering and project planning, 15 depots and 175 acres of freehold crane-parking land
- Stated wind-sector position - approximately 50-60% market share in India's wind sector and over 17 GW of cumulative installations supported (MD's message)
- Flagship execution credentials cited: Jamnagar Refinery Expansion (75 high-capacity cranes mobilised, zero-incident execution), Gati Shakti Highway Project Nagpur (700 MT girder across 72 m span using a 1,600 MT crawler crane), Narendra Modi Stadium Ahmedabad roof installation, Seabird Naval Base Karwar
- External rankings cited: 5th largest crane rental company worldwide (IC Index 2025) and largest in India and Asia; 6th largest worldwide (International Cranes IC Index, June 2023); 9th largest global crane-owning company (ICST Magazine, 2009)
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Competitive intensity in the domestic crane rental market — Explicitly listed under MD&A THREATS: 'Heightened competitive intensity in the domestic crane rental market, which may exert pressure on yields and margins despite sustained demand.' This bears directly on the two KPIs management runs the business on - average blended yield (2.12% per month) and fleet utilisation - and the MD&A concedes the Company relied on 'value-led customer engagement, disciplined asset deployment and calibrated commercial interventions to sustain yields and margins'.
- Import dependency for specialised equipment — MD&A THREATS: 'Reliance on specialised equipment imported from Germany and China exposes the Company to procurement delays, logistics risks, and potential changes in customs duties.' For an asset-heavy rental model where growth is delivered by adding high-capacity cranes, procurement lead-time or duty changes directly gate the capex programme; the MoU with Action Construction Equipment Limited for indigenously manufactured heavy cranes is the stated structural response.
- Execution and external delays causing order-book slippage — MD&A THREATS: 'Delays in project execution due to seasonal factors or customer site readiness may result in 10-15% of the order book carrying over into the next financial period.' This is a quantified, recurring revenue-recognition risk on a business whose visibility case rests on the order book, and it sits alongside the Rs 165 crore of FY2025-26 capex that was itself deferred to 2026-27.
- Revenue volatility in the EPC businesses under percentage-of-completion — MD&A THREATS and segment commentary: revenue can fluctuate in the EPC businesses because of the percentage-of-completion method, 'especially in the early stages of a project'. As the Wind EPC and Project EPC verticals are the stated diversification engines and are scaling from a low base, reported performance may vary between periods independent of underlying demand; the Company states it selects contracts on execution capability and profitability thresholds.
- Cost structure and localisation burden in new international geographies — MD&A THREATS: 'Higher operating costs in international markets such as Saudi Arabia, driven by manpower requirements, regulatory compliance, and localisation norms, impacting overall cost structures.' The segment commentary confirms that higher manpower, logistics and maintenance costs partly offset the superior Saudi yield advantage, with the Saudi business only beginning to generate positive monthly EBITDA - so the growth engine carries a margin-dilution risk while it scales.
- Single-activity and single-geography concentration — A structural concentration disclosed without being labelled a risk: BRSR Section A states crane hiring services account for 93.36% of turnover (Project EPC 6.63%), exports are 0% of turnover, and international markets served are stated as 0 countries. Notwithstanding the Saudi Arabia, Botswana and Qatar entities, the disclosed revenue base is overwhelmingly one activity in one country, so a domestic capex-cycle downturn or a single-sector demand shock transmits with little offset. (BRSR item 23 and the concentration items are read from the routed BRSR pages in this bundle.)
- Workforce attrition and occupational health & safety exposure — BRSR turnover rates jumped to 42.47% for permanent employees (18.22%/30.77%/19.06% split the prior year) and 77.00% for permanent workers (2.52% prior year) in FY2025-26 - the Company attributes this to Elevate 2030 growth and expansion. Separately, BRSR material issue 7 'Operational Health & Safety' flags accident, injury and fatality risk, 'especially among temporary workers who may lack sufficient training or experience', with serious incidents capable of causing project delays and downtime. For a business whose moat is stated to be execution and safety, a >40% attrition rate is a structural capability risk.
- Legacy indirect-tax litigation overhang — PROVENANCE: back-filled from the SIBLING capex_expansion bundle (Independent Auditor's Report CARO annexure, which arrived there mis-headed as BRSR); no litigation section was routed into this risks bundle. Disputed statutory dues on crane hiring remain unpaid under the Central Sales Tax Act 1956 (FY2010-11 to FY2017-18), Gujarat VAT 2003 (FY2008-09), Maharashtra VAT 2002 (FY2010-11 to FY2017-18) and multiple GST matters across Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha (FY2018-19 to FY2025-26), pending before the Bombay High Court, state sales tax tribunals, Joint/Additional Commissioners and GST appellate authorities. The auditor also reports provident-fund dues for May-August 2025 outstanding beyond six months and 'Not paid till date' as at March 31, 2026. Amounts deliberately not reproduced.

business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: SML supplies medium and heavy-duty cranes on a rental basis to private and public sector undertakings and delivers integrated lifting and project execution services, enabled by in-house engineering and project planning. The Group operates through three stated verticals: Crane Rental and Heavy Lift Solutions (the core vertical), Turnkey Solutions in Wind EPC (through Sangreen Future Renewables Private Limited), and Logistics for Cranes and Heavy Machinery (through Sangreen Logistics Private Limited), serving sectors such as renewables, logistics and core industries. It has moved from crane rental towards an integrated 'concept-to-commissioning' approach in wind energy, and has extended operations to Saudi Arabia and Botswana.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Elevate 2030 - a five-year guiding roadmap to transform SML from a predominantly single-line, India-centric crane rental company into a diversified, multi-business, globally aligned group; described as a 'dynamic blueprint for transformation'.
- Build multiple growth engines under Elevate 2030 so the business mix spans crane rentals, Wind EPC, Project EPC and international operations.
- Calibrated international expansion: Saudi Arabia established as the operating hub (globalisation track activated February 2025; go-to-market executed through Sanghvi Movers Middle East), with selective entry into Botswana and Qatar by 'following our customers' - entering with execution capability, building presence through delivery, and scaling in a calibrated manner.
- Remain firmly anchored in India as the stable, growing demand base while expanding abroad.
- Structure the renewable energy business under Sangreen Future Renewables Private Limited to give it a sharper operating model with dedicated leadership and clear P&L accountability.
- Move from crane rental to an integrated 'concept-to-commissioning' execution model in wind energy - repositioning from equipment provider to solution-oriented execution partner, reducing customer interface risk.
- Shift fleet management from project-based deployment to a portfolio-led approach where assets are managed across sectors and geographies as a unified system, enabling dynamic redeployment between renewables, nuclear and core industries.
- Forward-aligned planning rather than reactive deployment: position fleet in advance based on project timelines and sectoral demand to cut idle time, improve fleet rotation and stabilise utilisation.
- Fleet strategy aligned to complexity: direct expansion towards high-capacity cranes for renewables and nuclear, and standardise the fleet to improve interchangeability and asset productivity.
- Digital enablement - advance the enterprise-wide SAP rollout plus internal data-led demand forecasting, deployment planning and performance tracking, to move towards a predictive operating model.
- Institutionalise the organisation - transition from promoter-driven to a professional CXO-led model, with a full C-suite (CEO, CFO and other strategic functions) and dedicated leadership for Saudi operations.
- Financial discipline as strategy: the CFO states the financial strategy 'remains centred on maintaining a strong balance sheet, improving capital productivity, and enhancing earnings visibility', with capital deployment aligned to structural demand trends while preserving financial flexibility.
- Safety and governance as non-negotiable enablers of scale - strengthening governance frameworks, transparency and compliance as project complexity rises.
- Stated end-state: 'We are steadily moving towards becoming a group of companies, one that combines scale with capability, and growth with resilience.'
- The Board has formulated a Dividend Distribution Policy pursuant to Regulation 43A of the SEBI LODR, published on the Company's website. For FY2025-26 the AGM Notice puts a final dividend of Rs 2 per equity share to Members (Ordinary Business item 2). A subdivision of the equity shares is proposed, with a consequential special resolution altering the Articles of Association so that face value is linked to the Memorandum of Association - stated intent being to avoid further Article amendments whenever face value changes in future. PROVENANCE (back-filled from sibling bundles, because the routed governance text carries only the policy and the Notice item): the CFO frames financial strategy as 'maintaining a strong balance sheet, improving capital productivity, and enhancing earnings visibility', with capital deployment aligned to structural demand while preserving financial flexibility; Elevate 2030 names 'Financial Discipline - Driving capital efficiency and risk-managed growth' as one of six pillars and sets a capital-approach shift from asset-heavy to a hybrid model, alongside a ROCE ambition in the mid-teens range; the MD&A risk table states a debt-to-equity TARGET of 0.50x. The Strengths spread describes 'consistently low leverage and return-led capital allocation' as a structural advantage enabling investment ahead of demand. Specific rupee figures (payout ratio, cash outflow, leverage ratios) are deliberately excluded as financial-statement content.
- BRSR FY2025-26 carries NO external assurance - Section A item 14 'Name of assurance provider' and item 15 'Type of assurance obtained' are both printed as '-' (STATED NIL). Reporting boundary is standalone only (the listed entity), so the subsidiaries - including the renewables platform and the international entities - are outside the BRSR perimeter.
- Emissions & pollutants identified as a material RISK with negative financial implications: as a crane rental provider SML's operations involve significant energy use during crane operation, producing considerable direct and indirect GHG emissions. Stated mitigation: a defined environmental framework including investments in renewable energy installations such as solar power and deployment of energy-efficient equipment to enhance energy conservation and reduce carbon intensity.
- Climate risk and adaptation identified as a material RISK (physical risks such as floods and wildfires; transition risks such as mandatory renewable energy regulations). Stated response is continuous monitoring of evolving climate risks and regulatory developments - the AR states no emissions target, no net-zero date and no quantified climate commitment.
- Waste management identified as a material RISK, governed through a Waste Management Policy and an IT E-Waste Management Policy, stated to align with circular economy principles; 'Circular Economy' is separately listed as a material OPPORTUNITY with positive financial implications.
- Occupational health and safety run through ISO 45001-certified systems supported by a dedicated EHS framework, regular safety trainings, awareness initiatives and strict compliance with Standard Operating Procedures across all operational sites; safety is described by the MD as 'a non-negotiable priority'.
- Board diversity: 8 directors of whom 2 are female (25.00%). Key Management Personnel: 3, of whom 0 are female (printed as '-'). The KMP note states 'Total KMP includes the Managing Director and Whole-Time Directors'.
- Employee and worker turnover disclosed at 42.47% (permanent employees) and 77.00% (permanent workers) for FY2025-26 against 19.06% and 2.52% in FY2024-25 - a sharp deterioration the Company attributes to Elevate 2030 growth, expansion into new businesses and geographies, and normal business dynamics. Employee well-being and retention, and labour management, are both flagged as material risks.
- Grievance redressal mechanisms are in place for all six disclosed stakeholder groups with published web links (stakeholder engagement policy, vigil mechanism and whistle-blower policy, suppliers' code of conduct). FY2025-26 complaints: 1 from shareholders (non-receipt of shareholder list, resolved; nil pending at March 31, 2026) and 0 from communities, investors, employees and workers, customers and value chain partners. outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY2025-26 was a fleet- and geography-expansion year executed under the Elevate 2030 roadmap. The Corporate Overview 'New Developments' spread states the Company 'Revised 2025-26 CAPEX to Rs 639 crore', with Rs 415 crore allocated to India and Rs 224 crore allocated to Saudi Arabia, and focussed investments in high-capacity cranes (350 MT / 320 MT) to address demand in renewables and infrastructure. The MD&A separately states a total capital expenditure of Rs 474 crore incurred during 2025-26, comprising Rs 373 crore in India and Rs 101 crore in the Saudi Arabian subsidiary, with Rs 165 crore deferred to 2026-27; the MD&A also states the Rs 474 crore was invested 'in capability expansion, including the addition of 132 new cranes taking cumulative lifting capacity to 22,450 MTPA', and that a monetisation of 132 cranes took place during the year (the profit figure on that monetisation is a P&L item and is deliberately not reproduced). The two capex framings are recorded exactly as printed and are not reconciled - see notes. Geographic expansion: Saudi Arabia was operationalised through Sanghvi Movers Middle East, achieving go-to-market status with commercial operations commencing in September, over 30 cranes deployed directly from port to site at 100% utilisation, and 36 cranes added in the Saudi operation during FY2025-26 against capital expenditure of Rs 101 crore there; the MD has committed approximately Rs 225 crore towards scaling the Saudi fleet to upwards of 100 machines over the next 24 months, with an ambition of a top-tier position over five years and Saudi Arabia established as the operating hub with a pathway to GCC leadership. Africa entry was made through the first heavy-lift order in Botswana (Sanghvi Movers Botswana Proprietary Limited, Gaborone), and initial inquiries were received from Qatar (step-down subsidiary Sanghvi Movers Middle East Qatar Limited). Structurally, the renewables business was carved out into Sangreen Future Renewables Private Limited, and Sangreen Logistics Private Limited was set up for crane and heavy-machinery logistics. The Elevate 2030 'Financial Direction' anchors capital deployment of approximately Rs 500 crore alongside a revenue scale-up to Rs 1,800 crore by 2027-28, and the roadmap's 'Operating Scale' focus area commits to expanding the depot footprint and standardising the operating model. The physical footprint stated is 15 Company-owned depots across 12 states (BRSR states 15 states and 19 national offices, 0 plants), 175 acres of freehold land for crane parking, 4 regional offices and the registered office at Tathawade, Pune, with cranes operating at more than 130 customer locations across India as of March 31, 2026. Fleet is stated at 550+ cranes and 200+ specialised transport equipment (BRSR states 'over 450 cranes' with lifting capacities from 40 MT to 1600 MT); 1,600 MT crawler cranes were procured in 2024 and one was used for the largest ROB girder launch in the Company's history (700 MT over a 72 m span at Nagpur). An MoU was signed with Action Construction Equipment Limited (ACE) for deployment of indigenously manufactured heavy cranes in India.

outlook.body:
- Management states the domestic environment 'remains supportive of equipment rental demand, underpinning Sanghvi Movers' operating outlook amid ongoing global uncertainties', with India's growth expected to moderate but remain resilient, providing a predictable backdrop for long-term infrastructure and industrial activity.
- Industrial demand is being driven by technology-led investments, particularly high-tech manufacturing and data centres requiring specialised construction infrastructure; easing inflation is improving operating predictability.
- India crane rental industry projected to grow from US$ 2.86 Bn in 2025 to US$ 5.13 Bn by 2034 (CAGR 6.7%), supported by sustained infrastructure investment and renewable energy expansion.
- Structural shift to asset-light procurement: contractors increasingly favour rental models to optimise capital allocation and manage timelines, giving rental-based procurement structural traction; high equipment acquisition and maintenance costs, while a constraint, reinforce the attractiveness of rental.
- Infrastructure modernisation - metro rail operational or under construction in 23 cities spanning 1,013 km (as of May 2025), highways, bridges, smart cities and port-led development.
- Union Budget 2026-27 public capital expenditure raised to Rs 12.2 lakh crore (nearly 9% higher YoY), including Rs 3.10 lakh crore for MoRTH, Rs 1.87 lakh crore for NHAI and a record Rs 2.78 lakh crore for the Ministry of Railways - all equipment-intensive sectors.
- Renewable energy expansion as a structural growth driver: India renewable capacity 274.68 GW as of March 2026, wind capacity above 56 GW with a record 6.05 GW added in 2025-26; targets of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
- Nuclear pipeline: nuclear capacity 8.78 GW today against a target of 100 GW by 2047; power installed capacity 505 GW as of October 2025 with non-fossil at 259 GW (51.37%).
- Cement: CRISIL estimates 150-160 MT of new capacity to be added between 2025 and 2028; demand projected to grow 6.5-7.5% in 2025-26 - larger, more equipment-intensive projects.
- Steel: crude steel production up over 10.7% YoY to ~168.4 MT in 2025-26; India progressing towards ~300 MT steelmaking capacity by 2030-31 under National Steel Policy 2017.
- Oil & gas: refining capacity ~258 MMTPA as of January 2026 projected to reach ~309.56 MMTPA by 2028; gas share of the energy mix targeted at 15% by 2030 - technically intensive projects requiring heavy logistics.
- Saudi Arabia macro tailwind: real GDP growth projected at 4.5% in 2026, supported by Vision 2030 infrastructure pipeline; Botswana expected to return to growth from 2026 after a 0.9% contraction in 2025, with infrastructure and industrial investment sustaining demand for capital-intensive project execution.
- Margin/mix lever stated by the CFO: 'The revenue mix reflects a deliberate shift towards a more diversified portfolio, with increasing contributions from Wind EPC and Project EPC alongside the core Crane Rental business. This evolving mix is enhancing revenue visibility while progressively building execution-led and annuity-linked income streams.'
- Yield lever stated by the CEO: higher-capacity equipment is deployed on more specialised and higher-value assignments, contributing to better yield quality; in Saudi Arabia asset deployment is aligned to project readiness, optimising utilisation from the outset while maintaining strong yield profiles.
- Headwinds flagged in the same narrative: oil price volatility from the Iran-Israel-US conflict raising fuel and equipment transportation costs for operators near-term; global risks from high sovereign debt, geopolitical tension and potential volatility in high-tech investment; increased tariffs (US effective tariff rate 18.5%) and a rupee at around Rs 94-95/US$ as of April 2026.
- MD's message: 'This is reflected in our order book of approximately 1,053 crore as on May 14, 2026. The strength of this order book, supported by demand across sectors such as nuclear power, steel, cement, and hydrocarbons, provides both visibility and resilience.'
- CEO's message: 'our consolidated order book stood at approximately 1,053 crore as on May 14, 2026, with a substantial portion executable within the year, supported by an inquiry pipeline of Rs 4,000 crore across sectors such as renewables, metals, cement, and hydrocarbons.'
- CFO's message: 'The Company closed the year with a consolidated order book of Rs 1,070 crore, providing strong near-term revenue visibility. This is further supported by an inquiry pipeline in the range of Rs 4,000 crore.'
- The CEO states forward visibility has enabled a transition from reactive deployment to forward-aligned planning, reducing idle time between assignments and improving fleet rotation cycles.
- CONFLICT NOTED, NOT RESOLVED: the closing consolidated order book is stated as approximately Rs 1,053 crore (as on May 14, 2026) by both the MD and the CEO, and as Rs 1,070 crore by the CFO. Rs 1,070 crore is also the figure the CEO uses for consolidated total income from operations. Both order-book figures are reproduced as stated; neither is adjusted.

risks.note: Explicitly listed under MD&A THREATS: 'Heightened competitive intensity in the domestic crane rental market, which may exert pressure on yields and margins despite sustained demand.' This bears directly on the two KPIs management runs the business on - average blended yield (2.12% per month) and fleet utilisation - and the MD&A concedes the Company relied on 'value-led customer engagement, disciplined asset deployment and calibrated commercial interventions to sustain yields and margins'.
risks.risk: Competitive intensity in the domestic crane rental market

risks.note: MD&A THREATS: 'Reliance on specialised equipment imported from Germany and China exposes the Company to procurement delays, logistics risks, and potential changes in customs duties.' For an asset-heavy rental model where growth is delivered by adding high-capacity cranes, procurement lead-time or duty changes directly gate the capex programme; the MoU with Action Construction Equipment Limited for indigenously manufactured heavy cranes is the stated structural response.

MD&A THREATS: 'Delays in project execution due to seasonal factors or customer site readiness may result in 10-15% of the order book carrying over into the next financial period.' This is a quantified, recurring revenue-recognition risk on a business whose visibility case rests on the order book, and it sits alongside the Rs 165 crore of FY2025-26 capex that was itself deferred to 2026-27.
risks.risk: Execution and external delays causing order-book slippage

risks.note: MD&A THREATS and segment commentary: revenue can fluctuate in the EPC businesses because of the percentage-of-completion method, 'especially in the early stages of a project'. As the Wind EPC and Project EPC verticals are the stated diversification engines and are scaling from a low base, reported performance may vary between periods independent of underlying demand; the Company states it selects contracts on execution capability and profitability thresholds.
risks.risk: Revenue volatility in the EPC businesses under percentage-of-completion

risks.note: MD&A THREATS: 'Higher operating costs in international markets such as Saudi Arabia, driven by manpower requirements, regulatory compliance, and localisation norms, impacting overall cost structures.' The segment commentary confirms that higher manpower, logistics and maintenance costs partly offset the superior Saudi yield advantage, with the Saudi business only beginning to generate positive monthly EBITDA - so the growth engine carries a margin-dilution risk while it scales.
risks.risk: Cost structure and localisation burden in new international geographies

risks.note: A structural concentration disclosed without being labelled a risk: BRSR Section A states crane hiring services account for 93.36% of turnover (Project EPC 6.63%), exports are 0% of turnover, and international markets served are stated as 0 countries. Notwithstanding the Saudi Arabia, Botswana and Qatar entities, the disclosed revenue base is overwhelmingly one activity in one country, so a domestic capex-cycle downturn or a single-sector demand shock transmits with little offset. (BRSR item 23 and the concentration items are read from the routed BRSR pages in this bundle.)

BRSR turnover rates jumped to 42.47% for permanent employees (18.22%/30.77%/19.06% split the prior year) and 77.00% for permanent workers (2.52% prior year) in FY2025-26 - the Company attributes this to Elevate 2030 growth and expansion. Separately, BRSR material issue 7 'Operational Health & Safety' flags accident, injury and fatality risk, 'especially among temporary workers who may lack sufficient training or experience', with serious incidents capable of causing project delays and downtime. For a business whose moat is stated to be execution and safety, a >40% attrition rate is a structural capability risk.
risks.risk: Workforce attrition and occupational health & safety exposure
